All materials were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA) unless otherwise noted. The murine osteocytic cell line, Ocy454 was used in this experiment. The cell line was derived from double-transgenic immortalized mice (Immortomouse, Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington, MA, USA) expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under the dentin matrix protein 1 (Dmp1) promoter and a thermolabile simian virus 40 (SV40) large T antigen under the H-2Kb promoter, which is active at 33C (permissive temperature) and inactive at 37C (semi-permissive temperature). Ocy454 cells were grown at 33C with 5% CO2 on rat type I collagen-coated flasks (BioCoat, Corning, NY, USA) in the growth medium (minimum essential medium α supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% antibiotic- antimycotic). Upon reaching 80% confluence, cells were trypsinized with TrypLE Express and seeded on highly porous 200 μm-thick polystyrene 3D scaffolds (Alvetex 6-well insert, ~18 mm diameter) (Reprocell, Sedgefield, Co. Durham, UK) at a density of 1.6 × 10^6 cells/scaffold. The scaffolds were cultured in the growth medium for 3 days at 33C with 5% CO2, and then fed with fresh growth medium and incubated for an additional 2 days under 37C with 5% CO2 to initiate the osteocytic differentiation. Three days prior to launch (−3 d) the cell-containing scaffolds were punched to a diameter of 9 mm with trephine blades (Bausch & Lomb Storz, Bridgewater, NJ, USA), and five 9 mm scaffolds were randomly housed in a flight-certified bioreactor (described below). The bioreactors were then integrated into fluid flight-certified pathways followed by feeding with 5 mL of fresh growth medium and overnight incubation under 37C with 5% CO2.

The details about the flight-certified cell culture hardware, eOSTEO (enhanced Osteoporosis Experiments on Orbit), were previously described. Briefly, eOSTEO, originally designed by Canadian Space Agency (CSA), is a fully automated cell culture system developed by CALM Technologies (Kingston, ON, Canada) and successfully flown in previous spaceflight missions including OSTEO-3. For the OSTEO-4 mission, the eOSTEO payload was further modified by CALM Technologies to meet the requirements onboard the ISS. The modified payload, OSTEO-4, was composed of three layers of independent cell culture trays and each tray housed three removable bioreactors that were connected to any of five 60 mL syringe reservoirs via a silicone tube fluid pathway. The OSTEO-4 payload operates a closed system that does not allow for the free exchange of oxygen and CO2, hence three of the five syringes were filled with the growth medium supplemented with 25 mM HEPES buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) to preserve the pH of the medium. Ground-based preliminary experiments demonstrated that growth medium for OSTEO-4 experiments supplemented with 25 mM HEPES buffer maintained physiological pH in the non-CO2 closed environment for up to 24 hours between 5-mL medium re-feeds without any significant effects on osteocytic gene expression. The remaining two syringes were filled with either RNA stabilizer (RNAprotect Cell Reagent, Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA) or 0.99% paraformaldehyde (PFA, Acros, Fair Lawn, NJ, USA) in Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline (DPBS, General Electric, Logan, UT, USA). We prepared two identical OSTEO-4 payloads, one was for the spaceflight and the other served as a ground control, with the random-integration of the fluid pathways including bioreactors and five syringes into the flight or ground control cell culture trays to minimize sample bias. An additional ground control was prepared two days later, following identical protocols, and used as supplemental control samples. Forty-eight hours before launch (−2 d) the flight OSTEO-4 payload was handed over to the NASA team and launched into space on board the CRS-6 SpaceX Dragon spacecraft from Cape Canaveral, FL, on April 14th, 2015. The two identical ground control OSTEO-4 payloads were kept in the ISS chamber at Kennedy Space Center which mimiced the temperature and humidity conditions of Dragon-6 and ISS. For the entire duration of the experiment, the cell culture bioreactors were maintained at 37C and automatically fed with the HEPES-containing growth medium (5 mL per bioreactor) at 28 and 23 hours prior to launch (due to one day delay of launch) and every 24 hours after launch The bioreactors were fixed with either RNA stabilizer or 0.99% PFA in DPBS at 2, 4, or 6 days of exposure to μG conditions and were subsequently cooled down to 8-16C prior to being disconnected from the cell culture trays along with media collection bags and stored in the cold stowage (−80C) on the ISS by astronauts. The bioreactors and media samples were returned to earth maintaining cold-stowage condi- tions on the same Dragon-6 spacecraft on May 21st, 2015.     Total RNA was isolated using RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Briefly, the bioreactors frozen and fixed with RNA stabilizer (RNAprotect Cell Reagent, Qiagen) at different time points (2, 4, or 6 days) under 1G or μG were thawed for 45-60 min- utes at room temperature. From each bioreactor, three of five 9-mm-punched 3D cell culture scaffolds (Alvetex, Reprocell) were removed and individually re-stored in fresh RNA stabilizer at −80C for later analysis. To optimize cell lysing, each of the remaining two scaffolds was cut into half and both pieces were lysed together in 1.7 mL RNase-free microcentrifuge tubes (Denville Scientific, Holliston, MA, USA) containing 650 μL of Buffer RLT Plus (RNeasy Plus Mini Kit, Qiagen) supplemented with 1% β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich) by agitating at 2000 rpm for 10 minutes at room temperature with a thermal mixer (Thermal Mixer II, Fisher Scientific). The lysed cell samples and the remaining scaffolds were then transferred in QIAshredder spin columns (Qiagen) and centrifuged at 16 100× g for 3 minutes at room temperature for homog- enization. The homogenized samples were further processed with a genomic DNA elimination step by following the Qiagen's RNA isolation protocol. Isolated total RNA both from spaceflight and ground control samples were high qual- ity and integrity, as determined by the 28S/18S rRNA peak and area ratios (ranges 1.8-2.1 and 1.9-2.5, respectively) and the RNA integrity number (RIN, range 8.2-8.7) using RNA 6000 Pico Assay RNA chips run in Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA). The RNA sam- ples were stored at −80C until further analysis.     Briefly, total RNA (100 ng) was reverse- transcribed using GeneChip WT Plus Reagent Kit. The obtained double-stranded cDNA was used as a template for in vitro transcription (IVT) resulting in antisense cRNA which was purified using Purification Beads and used as a template for reverse transcription to produce single-stranded DNA in the sense orientation. During this step 2′-deoxyuridine-5′-triphosphate (dUTP) was incorporated. The DNA was then fragmented using uracil DNA glyco- sylase (UDG) and apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE 1) and labeled with DNA Labeling Reagent that is covalently linked to biotin using terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT). IVT and cDNA fragmentation quality controls were carried out by running an mRNA Pico assay in the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer.     The labeled fragmented DNA was hybridized to the Mouse Transcriptome Arrays 1.0 for 16-18 hours in GeneChip Hybridization Oven 640 at 45°C with rotation at 60 rpm. The hybridized samples were washed and stained using Affymetrix fluidics station 450. The first stain with streptavidin-R-phycoerythrin (SAPE) was followed by signal amplification using a biotinylated goat anti-streptavidin antibody and another SAPE staining (Hybridization, Washing and Staining Kit).     GeneChip Microarrays were immediately scanned using Affymetrix GeneArray Scanner 3000 7G Plus.     Mouse Transcriptome Array CEL files were normalized to produce probeset-level expression values using the implementation of the Robust Multiarray Average (RMA) in the Affymetrix Expression Console software package. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed using the prcomp R function with expression values that had been normalized across all samples to a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.     Analyses of variance were performed using the f.pvalue function in the sva package (version 3.4.0). Pairwise differential expression was assessed using by performing Student's t test on the co- efficients of linear models created using the lmFit function in the limma package (version 3.14.4). Correction for multiple hypothesis testing was accomplished using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR). All microarray analyses were performed using the R environment for statistical computing (version 2.15.1).

_source.Study Description: Bone loss is one of the major health problems for astronauts during long-term spaceflight and for patients during prolonged bed rest or paralysis. Growing evidence suggests that osteocytes, the most abundant cells in the mineralized bone matrix, play a key role in sensing mechanical forces applied to the skeleton and in transducing them into subcellular biochemical signals to modulate bone homeostasis. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying both mechanosensation and mechanotransduction in osteocytes under the real microgravity (µG) condition are poorly understood. To unravel the mechanisms by which osteocyte, sense and responds to mechanical unloading, we exposed murine osteocytic cell line, Ocy454, seeded on a highly porous polystyrene 3D scaffold, to 2, 4, or 6 days of µG on board the International Space Station (ISS) and compared their gene expression with cells at 1G on Earth. Bioinformatics analysis of cells exposed to µG revealed several pathways differentially regulated upon exposure to microgravity.

_source.Study Protocol Description:
Rodent Research Reference Mission 1 (RRR-1) / Rodent Research-8 (RR-8) consisted of 40 BALB/cAnNTac females (8 used for this study) termed Flight which were sent on 12/5/2018 to the International Space Station (ISS), and a control group of 40 mice remained on Earth, termed Habitat Ground Control (HC). Furthermore, two age groups were used, younger (∼3 months) and older (∼8 months). All mouse work was completed with approval of the NASA Flight Animal Care and Use Committee (Protocol FLT-18-116). Mice were received following landing at Scripps Research Institute (09-0004, for animal receipt upon landing) and transported to Stanford University IACUC (WYS1591). Flight mice were housed at double density on launch and again during the return to earth. HC mice were housed to match, as closely as possible, conditions experienced by Flight mice. This included double density housing in identical Mouse Habitat Units and Transporters as used by NASA during launch for Flight mice, and matched temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide levels (elevated on the ISS compared to Earth) based on actual flight environmental monitoring. All mice were adapted to NASA Nutrient Food Bars, four weeks prior to launch, and bars were exchanged weekly. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. Mice had ad libitum access to both food and water. During the mission we encountered the following issues, altering the planned experimental design, or that must be considered upon interpretation of results. (1) Within 24h of the planned launch, mold was found on the food bars, affecting both Flight and HGC mice to an unknown degree. It is possible that the mice were able to eat around the mold. The late replacement of the food bars, now secured with double-sided tape instead of epoxy, caused the bars to free-float during launch and return. The bars of the HGC mice fell to the bottom of the cage. Although the Flight mice appeared healthy upon arrival to the ISS, this might have induced additional stress. Due to concerns about mold, as more was discovered aboard the ISS, the ISS Term mice were sacrificed after approximately 3 weeks of microgravity rather than the planned 8 weeks, and ground controls were sacrificed to match this new timeline.(2) Due to poor weather, the return of the Flight LAR mice was delayed and the mice spent 7 instead of the normal 2-3 days in double density housing. This housing is more confined (10 mice per cage side instead of the 5 in the normal habitat), video monitoring was not possible and food bars likely became unsecured and were free-floating. Conditions of the HGC mice were matched to these conditions, likely causing additional stress for both groups. Due to the weather, the Flight group likely experienced rough seas upon splashdown and shipping back to shore, which was not controlled for in the HGC group.     HC mice were shipped to Scripps Institute just prior to the return of the Flight mice so that all mice could be dissected together in matching conditions (+/- 1 day). The mice from the Flight group were returned alive to Earth on 1/14/2019 after 39.5 days on the ISS and collected 2-4 days after splashdown following functional assays at Scripps Research Institute. In this study, fresh organ samples were obtained and immediately processed from 8 live mice that arrived at Stanford University from Scripps Research Institute on 1/16/2019. Two mice each from the following groups were included: Flight 3mo, Flight 8mo, HC 3mo, HC 8mo. All four Flight mice were dissected on 1/16/2019 to minimize time spent outside of microgravity, and all four HC mice dissected on 1/17/2019. LAR mice were anesthetized with gas anesthesia and euthanized by means of cardiac puncture blood draw (exsanguination) and double thoracotomy.     All the tissues were processed as previously described (https://doi.org:10.1038/s41586-020-2496-1). Muscle cells collected from hindlimbs and forelimbs were prepared for FACS isolation as described96. In brief, muscles from each mouse were minced and digested in 10 ml 2 mg/ml collagenase II (Worthington LS004179) at 37 C for 1 hour with agitation followed by a second digestion with 1,000 Units of collagenase II and 11 Units of dispase (Thermo Fisher 17105-041) for 30 minutes. The digested tissues were then passed through a 20-gauge needle to release mononucleated cells. The resulting cell suspension was filtered with a 40 µm strainer (Falcon cat.
352340) and pelleted. Cells were then resuspended in 0.5 ml wash medium (Ham's F-10 (Thermo Fisher SH30025.01) supplemented with 10% (vol/vol) horse serum (Invitrogen 16050-122) and 1× penicillin-streptomycin (Omega Scientific PS-20)) and stained with 1:1000 CD31-APC (BioLegend 102510), 1:1000 CD45-FITC (BioLegend 103108), 1:250 Ly-6A/E-PB (BioLegend 108120), and 1:100 CD106-PE/Cy7 (BioLegend 105720) at 4C for 30 minutes. Cells were washed once in wash medium before FACS isolation. Cells were sorted into 4 bins: satellite cells (Vcam1+, Sca1-, CD31-, CD45-), mesenchymal progenitors (Sca1+, CD31-, CD45-), endothelial cells CD31+, CD45-), and immune cells (CD45+).     Cells were loaded in each channel with a target output of up to 5,000 cells per sample, though fewer cells were captured for small sample types. scRNA-seq libraries were constructed following the 10x Genomics protocol using the GemCode Single-Cell 3’ Gel Bead and Library v3 Kit. All reactions were performed in a Biorad C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler with a 96-Deep Well Reaction Module. Twelve cycles were used for cDNA amplification and sample index PCR. Amplified cDNA and final libraries were evaluated on a Fragment Analyzer using a High Sensitivity NGS Analysis Kit (Advanced Analytical). Library preparation was performed one organ type at a time, in sets of eight samples. Within each organ set, cDNA was normalized, and 13–20 PCR cycles were run depending on cDNA amount. The average fragment length of 10x cDNA libraries was quantified on a Fragment Analyzer (AATI) and by qPCR using the Kapa Library Quantification Kit for Illumina. Each library was diluted to 4 nM, and equal volumes were pooled for each sequencing run.     Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using 100-cycle run kits, with 28 bases for Read 1, 8 bases for Index 1, and 91 bases for Read 2 (Illumina 20012862). A PhiX control library was spiked in at 0.2–1%.     Fastq format was checked with fastq_utils v0.25.1. Quality assessment of reads was performed with FastQC v0.11.9 and reports were combined with MultiQC v1.12. rRNA percentages of reads were estimated with the 'hts_SeqScreener' program of htstream v1.3.3 screened against a fasta file of Mus-musculus rRNA sequences retrieved from NCBI on 09-May-2025.
_source.Study Description: Spaceflights significantly impacts astronaut health, causing muscle atrophy, bone loss, cardiovascular deconditioning and immune system dysregulation, especially during long missions. To explore molecular changes, we generated a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset, of 216 samples from 28 mouse organs and tissues under spaceflight and control conditions. Since spaceflight effects closely resemble aspects of aging, we included two age groups (3 and 8 months) to assess age-related influences. Our data revealed that spaceflight drives age-independent systemic changes, primarily affecting tissue remodeling and alterations in cytoskeleton, membrane and extracellular matrix (ECM), particularly in endothelial cells. In contrast, aging has a weaker impact, mainly altering immune regulation in an age-dependent manner. These findings suggest that cytoskeletal and ECM changes may contribute to immune Dysregulation.
